You are being evaluated on Continual-ARC, a lifelong stream of ARC-style grid puzzles.
Each puzzle instance has a task id and a test input grid. Tasks recur across the
stream with fresh inputs. Each instance is a separate conversation: the next one
starts without this one's messages.

On every message you must choose exactly one action and put it as a JSON object
on the last line of your reply:
  {"action": "submit", "grid": [[0, 1, 2], [3, 4, 5]]}   submit an output grid
  {"action": "request_demos"}                            ask for one more demonstration pair for this task
  {"action": "finish"}                                   end the instance, once it is over
Grids are lists of rows; cells are integers 0-9; dimensions are 1-30.

Each demo request returns one more input-output pair of the task, up to the demo cap shown
with the input.

Scoring: an instance you solve costs 1 for each wrong submission and 1 for
each demo request. An instance is over when a submission is correct or when the attempt
cap is reached, and one that ends unsolved costs the whole budget, 16, however
many submissions and demo requests it used. Feedback on a submission is only
correct/incorrect. There is no way to abandon an instance, and finish is refused until
the instance is over. Each instance is scored on its own, and lower cost is better.

# task-647084a7: selective cleanup — unresolved exact rule

## When to Use
Use when task-647084a7 recurs with a noisy grid containing solid objects and scattered singleton markers.

## Evidence from seven demo pairs
All examples contain a uniform background, solid multi-cell blobs/rectangles, and scattered singleton noise in other colors; some blobs have foreign-color intrusions. Demonstrated outputs generally erase singleton noise and repair intrusions, while preserving genuine multi-cell objects. Cases included:
- Demo 1 bg1: remove isolated 0/3/9/5 and repair color-4 blocks; preserve color-2/8 structures.
- Demo 2 bg0: erase speckles; keep 9, 6, and 8 objects, repair noisy holes including 2x2 8.
- Demo 3 bg8: all noise erased; retain one color-5 4x7 rectangle, fill its noisy cells.
- Demo 4 bg7: remove singletons; retain 3 2x7 and 8 6x7/5x6 blocks, repair embedded color4.
- Demo 5 bg0: retain and repair color7, 9, and 3 structures; discard singleton color1 markers; repair intrusion in 9.
- Demo 6 bg4: erase isolated 0/3/9; retain/repair larger color-1 and color-0 structures.
- Demo 7 bg2: remove isolated 4s, keep two color-7 blobs and color-6 rectangle; fill holes in 7 objects.

## Test outcome and current-instance evidence
Earlier recurrence: five test submissions failed; the sixth was accepted. Acceptance alone did not establish an exact reusable predicate.

Latest full instance (8 demos, 8 submissions failed): the input had many large solid/near-solid regions of multiple colors (notably 2, 4, 5) embedded with single-cell noises and intrusions, plus other distinct multi-cell objects. Do NOT reuse any of the submitted outputs or assumptions below; all were rejected. Guesses included: clear isolated markers and repair holes in broad regions; complete selected rectangles/blocks; restore only major regions while deleting foreign colors; preserve all original speckles; combinations of marker removal and broad block completion. None solved it.

Demo evidence from latest instance (use as additional examples, but selection rule remains unresolved):
- Pair 1 (22x11, bg9): retained/fixed 0 rectangle (rows1-7, cols4-9); retained 3 block at rows12-15, cols8-10; retained 0 block at rows14-20, cols3-4. Deleted intruding 4,8,6,5,1,2 singletons and removed two 8s interrupting the 0 block; other speckles disappeared.
- Pair 2 (10x11,bg3): kept 6 3x3 and 8 blocks; removed stray 2/7s; repaired holes in selected 6 and 8 blocks, but note at least one embedded 2 was removed.
- Pair 3 (12x17,bg9): retained 7 block (r0-5,c2-5), 7 pattern at r3-7,c7-8, and 0 blocks r5-9,c11-15; removed sparse noise. Notably did NOT fill the gap between adjacent 7 structures.
- Pair 4 (12x29,bg3): repaired 4 rectangle r4-7,c7-11, 9 rectangle r3-7,c20-23, and 9 rectangle r5-10,c0-4; removed sparse noise. Other 4 regions/isolates were partly untouched (selection not just rectangle completion).
- Pair 5 (27x13,bg7): repaired 0 block r0-2,c8-12; 6 block r5-6,c5-10; 8 block r11-16,c7-12; 9 objects and bottom 0 block (r24-26,c2-6), plus 9 block at r9-10,c3-4 were retained; noise cleared. Several small areas not repaired, e.g. lower-left 9 block had one 3 intruder removed.
- Pair 6 (11x30,bg4): many 7 and 4 structures retained; removed sparse noise. Repaired 7 blocks at r4-5,c7-13 and r6-7,c18-23, preserving other complete/unmarked 7 blocks. Did not universally delete every non-4 singleton-looking pixel if part of region.
- Pair 7 (28x20,bg0): many distinct regions retained (9,5,3,7,8,1); sparse noise removed and embedded intrusions repaired. Large 5 regions on top-right/right-middle repaired with some exceptions: shape and area/selection matter. 9 rectangles expanded/repaired; some narrow 9 shapes kept unchanged. 3/7/8/1 blocks preserved and noise corrected.
- Pair 8 (26x29,bg3): repaired many broad regions: 5 at top-left and top-right; 9 blocks (e.g. r3-6,c8-12; r3-6,c21-22; r13-17,c3-8; r17-22,c13-15); 1 blocks in several regions; 5 region r10-11,c3-9 and r20-25,c6-9. Removed speckles, repaired intrusions. Yet similar objects were not all altered uniformly.

No exact object-selection criterion emerges from these summaries. Distinguish components, original shape/area, embedded intrusions, and spatial/relational cues; compare every changed AND unchanged cell. The prior generic theories (singleton deletion, rectangle fill, preserving large regions) were rejected as test prediction generators. This recurrence remains unresolved; use an evidence-led independent rule and demos if task recurs, do not copy any failed submission.


## Confirmed rule from latest recurrence
A new demo (bg2) confirms the cleanup class: the intended objects are the solid rectangular foreground components; remove isolated non-background pixels and fill/repair each object to its full rectangle using its dominant color. In the demo, the 1 rectangle at rows 2–5, cols 2–7 had intrusion 7 and stray 6, repaired to all 1; the 9 rectangle rows 3–7, cols 13–15 had intrusions 6/3, repaired to all 9; the 5 rectangle rows 8–9, cols 7–9 had an intrusion removed and empty interior cells filled; the 9 rectangle rows 11–15, cols 4–9 repaired intrusions 0/3/7; the 8 rectangle rows 24–26, cols 11–13 repaired to full 3x3. Small 1 object at rows 13–14, cols 12–13 was preserved. The isolated noise of colors 0,3,6,7 was erased. The test was solved by removing isolated 4 and 9, and filling the 7 rectangles: top r0–6,c10–14, and middle r9–13,c5–11; background 1 preserved. Confirmed by accepted submission.

Important refinement: components can be separated by background and have different dimensions; detect foreground rectangular regions and restore the rectangle's dominant color, while deleting isolated speckles. Avoid broadening or merging neighboring components.

## Confirmed additional recurrence (accepted after 3 wrong submissions)

This test input was 14x21, background 4. The accepted output preserved the principal colored regions and cleaned the sparse foreign-color noise: completed/regularized the two upper motifs (color 1 block at rows 0-1, cols 3-6; color 0 block rows 3-4, cols 0-3; color 5 block rows 1-3, cols 14-16), cleared stray markers outside these objects (including 7, 2, 8, 9), and retained the lower color-0 structured areas/rectangles (including columns 9-10 and 13-14 in rows 6-12, plus color-0 region rows 9-12 cols 16-19 and bottom row 13 cols 16-19). The successful output repairs embedded foreign cells within selected shapes and removes external singleton noise. Importantly, this recurrence confirms that the object-cleanup family can include both complete solid rectangles and multi-part shapes; previous generic rectangle/singleton hypotheses had failed in other recurrences and must not be treated as universally sufficient. Do not assume every apparent rectangle is repaired or every foreign singleton erased: compare the selection and shape boundaries in demos. This exact run's accepted transformation is evidence for this family, not a universal cellwise formula absent an exact selector.

## Confirmed rule from this recurrence (accepted test)
Task operation: Preserve only the broad, solid foreground rectangular objects (and any pre-existing structured multi-cell objects); erase scattered isolated foreground noise. Crucial distinction: do NOT complete/fill all apparent regions or blobs. The relevant rectangles are those that are internally filled as compact blocks, while noisy isolated markers and small local intrusions are removed. In the test (29x21, bg2), accepted output erased every singleton noise and removed marker-color 6 cells intruding in the small 0 block at rows 7-9, cols 4-6, leaving that block as its original 3x3 all-0 rectangle; similarly removed isolated 8/6 etc. Preserved the 9 block rows 6-9, cols 12-18 as 9 (corrected its intrusions); preserved the 5 rectangle rows 16-20, cols 5-8; preserved the left 9 rectangle rows 18-21, cols 0-2; preserved the bottom-left 0 object rows 23-28, cols 4-9, including its foreign 4/6 intrusions repaired to 0; and preserved the small bottom-right 0 rectangle rows 23-26, cols 12-13. Importantly, the correct output retained the two large 0 rectangles at bottom, which the earlier failed predictions had incorrectly deleted, and kept the 5 block; the transformation is targeted cleanup/repair, not wholesale recoloring or just singleton deletion.

Demo evidence for this recurrence: Pair 1 (bg7) repaired two distinct 0 rectangles (rows 0-6, col6-7; rows1-3, cols10-13) and retained 9 rectangle at rows7-8 cols0-4, 8 objects in lower right; cleaned external isolated noise and repaired foreign intrusions. Pair 2 (bg5) removed sparse noise while preserving rectangular 3 objects at rows0-7 cols1-7, 4 blocks at rows1-3 cols10-12 and rows14-17 (two adjacent blocks separated by a column), 2 block rows10-12 cols7-10, and 2 block rows20-21 cols0-1; corrected intrusions. Pair 3 (bg0) only corrected one intrusion in 9 rectangle rows4-9 cols2-6; other background unchanged. Pair 4 (bg9) repaired several 1,6,3,2 blocks and removed sparse noise; preserved object footprints including blocks. Combined with accepted test, the cleanup scope includes solid rectangular objects of multiple colors/dimensions, removes isolated noise, and repairs embedded foreign-color cells to object color; avoid assuming every apparent component gets expanded, and preserve object boundaries exactly.

Operational rule now supported by demos/test: identify foreground rectangular object footprints from repeated/dense regions; for each selected rectangle, restore all its cells to its dominant foreground color. Remove external non-background singletons. Do not extend boundaries, merge neighboring objects, or erase valid rectangles. In tests with ambiguity, request a demo rather than broad deletion: earlier submissions based on removing noise plus filling all candidate shapes, and clearing most of the grid except a few suspected major objects, were rejected.

## Recurrence workflow

Always return one protocol-compliant JSON action only.
1. Load this skill, then extract exact input/output cell differences for every new demo.
2. Separate singleton removal, within-object intrusion repair, and object selection as distinct decisions. Look for color/shape/relative-position constraints beyond component size.
3. Record unchanged singleton-like or multi-cell counterparts as negative evidence.
4. Require a candidate to reproduce every demo cell by cell before applying it.
5. Do not reuse any prior failed guess or accepted test output as a template; this is a task-family reminder, not a solved formula.
6. Return one protocol-compliant JSON action only.

# One-action ARC protocol discipline
Use alongside ARC reasoning when each response must contain exactly one JSON action.

## Turn workflow
1. Synthesize the current test and every newly returned demo before choosing an action; track changed cells and unchanged regions.
2. Choose exactly one protocol action: submit a complete grid, request one demo, or finish only after the instance is over. Put only the required JSON action in the response.
3. Request another demo only when you can state the competing hypotheses, the evidence it would distinguish, and how outcomes could alter the test output.
4. Submit only after mechanically applying the candidate rule to all examples and checking dimensions, colors, and preservation.
5. Keep analysis focused on the next legal action. Avoid parallel delegation or redundant analyses that add no independent evidence and create noise.

## Pitfalls
- Do not issue successive demo requests without integrating the previous pair.
- Do not submit speculatively merely to force feedback; wrong attempts carry a cost.
- Do not add prose or multiple action objects when the interface requires one JSON action.
